hero.heading: Does your AI fall under the EU regulation?
hero.lede: Answer the questions a lawyer would ask. At the end you get the classification — with the provision of the law it rests on.
start.heading: The classification starts with three questions about the system
start.intro: After that, the helper only asks what your answers leave open. At the end you get the risk class, the reasoning and the provision of the law.
start.method: Nothing is guessed: the classification follows from your answers and the published rule set, not from a language model. That is why every question carries the paragraph number of the official interpretation it rests on.
start.privacy: None of your answers leave your device. No server, no sign-up, no storage.
start.source: The questions follow the text of the regulation and the draft guidelines of the European Commission of 19 May 2026 line by line. Each one names the paragraph it rests on.

faq.heading: Frequently asked questions about the AI Act
faq.1.question: Does our recruiting tool fall under the EU AI Act?
faq.1.answer: Yes, as soon as it screens or filters applications, evaluates candidates or ranks them. Annex III point 4(a) of the AI Act expressly lists the recruitment and selection of natural persons, including the placing of targeted job advertisements. This applies to employees as well as to self-employed persons and platform workers. A tool that only processes applications descriptively, such as converting file formats, is not covered.
faq.2.question: What is a high-risk AI system?
faq.2.answer: The AI Act has two routes to it. Under Article 6(1), a system is high-risk if it is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I — machinery, toys, lifts, medical devices, vehicles — and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment. Under Article 6(2), it is high-risk if its intended purpose falls into one of the eight areas of Annex III: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, administration of justice.
faq.3.question: Are we a provider or a deployer?
faq.3.answer: A provider develops an AI system and places it on the market under its own name. A deployer uses it under its own authority. The difference determines the obligations: Article 16 applies to the provider, Article 26 to the deployer. Whoever substantially modifies a purchased system or offers it under their own name becomes a provider under Article 25.
faq.4.question: Which deadlines apply under the EU AI Act?
faq.4.answer: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 has been in force since 1 August 2024. The prohibited AI practices under Article 5 and the AI literacy obligation under Article 4 have applied since 2 February 2025. The obligations for general-purpose AI models have applied since 2 August 2025. The obligations for high-risk AI systems under Annex III apply from 2 August 2026, those for high-risk AI systems under Annex I from 2 August 2027.
faq.5.question: How high are the fines?
faq.5.answer: Article 99 sets them in tiers. For prohibited AI practices under Article 5, up to EUR 35 million or 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. For infringements of the obligations for high-risk AI systems, up to EUR 15 million or 3 %. For supplying incorrect information to authorities, up to EUR 7.5 million or 1 %.
faq.6.question: Is emotion recognition in the workplace allowed?
faq.6.answer: No. Article 5(1)(f) prohibits AI systems that infer the emotions of natural persons in the workplace or in education institutions. Medical and safety reasons are exempt, such as detecting fatigue in drivers or pilots. A prohibition outweighs a classification: the system must not be operated in that way.
faq.7.question: We use ChatGPT in our company. What do we have to do?
faq.7.answer: As the deployer of a purchased system, you are subject to the AI literacy obligation under Article 4 and, if the system is used for a purpose listed in Annex III, the deployer obligations under Article 26. The obligation to mark generated content under Article 50(2) applies to the provider of the model, not to you. As a deployer, you must disclose under Article 50(4) when you publish deep fakes or publish text on matters of public interest without human review.
faq.8.question: What is the exemption under Article 6(3)?
faq.8.answer: A system that falls into an area of Annex III is exceptionally not considered high-risk if it only performs a narrow procedural task, only improves the result of a previously completed human activity, only detects decision-making patterns or only performs a preparatory task. The exemption never applies if the system performs profiling of natural persons. Whoever relies on it must document the assessment and still register the system.
faq.9.question: Does credit scoring fall under the EU AI Act?
faq.9.answer: Evaluating the creditworthiness of natural persons falls under Annex III point 5(b). Systems whose main purpose is detecting financial fraud are excluded. Credit checks on companies are not covered, as long as the personal finances of an individual are not assessed at the same time.
faq.10.question: Do we need a data protection impact assessment?
faq.10.answer: The AI Act and the General Data Protection Regulation apply side by side. If your system processes personal data and is high-risk, a data protection impact assessment under Article 35 of the General Data Protection Regulation is usually called for. If the system takes automated decisions with legal effects, Article 22 of the General Data Protection Regulation applies as well.
areas.heading: The eight areas of Annex III
areas.intro: If the intended purpose of your system falls into one of these areas, it is a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2) — subject to the exemption in Article 6(3).
areas.1.name: Biometrics
areas.1.text: Remote biometric identification, biometric categorisation according to sensitive attributes, emotion recognition.
areas.2.name: Critical infrastructure
areas.2.text: Safety components in the supply of electricity, gas, heating and water, in road traffic and in critical digital infrastructure.
areas.3.name: Education and vocational training
areas.3.text: Access and admission, evaluation of learning outcomes, assessment of the level of education, monitoring during tests.
areas.4.name: Employment and workers management
areas.4.text: Recruitment and selection, promotion, termination, task allocation, monitoring of performance and behaviour.
areas.5.name: Essential private and public services
areas.5.text: Public assistance benefits, creditworthiness, risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance, emergency calls and triage.
areas.6.name: Law enforcement
areas.6.text: Risk of becoming a victim or offender, polygraphs, evaluation of evidence, profiling.
areas.7.name: Migration, asylum and border control management
areas.7.text: Polygraphs, risk assessment of persons entering, examination of applications, identification.
areas.8.name: Administration of justice and democratic processes
areas.8.text: Assisting judicial authorities, influencing elections and referendums.
sources.heading: Where the answers come from
sources.intro: Every question of this tool and every example carries the paragraph number of the passage it rests on. The tool works with three sources:
sources.aiAct.name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
sources.aiAct.text: Laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence, official text from the Official Journal of 12 July 2024 in German and English — 1386 individually addressable passages.
sources.gdpr.name: Regulation (EU) 2016/679
sources.gdpr.text: The General Data Protection Regulation, official text in German and English — 1024 passages.
sources.guidelines.name: Draft guidelines of the European Commission of 19 May 2026
sources.guidelines.text: On the classification of high-risk AI systems — 148 pages on Annex III, 13 pages on Annex I, 6 pages of general principles. They are the source of 379 questions, 214 explicit exclusions and 187 official examples shown next to the finding for comparison. The helper is measured against all 217 official examples of the draft.
sources.caveat: The draft guidelines are not binding. The public consultation ran until 23 June 2026; no final version was available when this work was completed. This tool does not replace legal advice.
software.heading: For your own computer
software.text: The same classification is available as a program for Windows, Mac and Linux. It adds full-text search in the text of the regulation: ask a question in your own words, and the helper shows the passages of the regulation that answer it. Install, start, done — no Python, no setup, no sign-up.

org.guide.skill1: Legal text transferred line by line

bench.heading: Measured against the European Commission
bench.lede: In its draft guidelines the Commission gives its own verdict for every example. The helper got only the description, the way a user knows their system. Every figure here is recounted from the measurement logs in the source code.
bench.headline.text: official examples classified the same way as the Commission
bench.verdicts.heading: By the Commission's verdict
bench.steps.heading: Steps to the finding
bench.parity.heading: Web page and program compute the same
bench.parity.text: random runs with identical questions, identical order and identical finding.
bench.parity.takeaway: The same logic exists twice in the code: once in Python, once in JavaScript. Without this check two versions drift apart; before every package build every run must agree.
bench.tests.heading: Automated tests
bench.tests.text: tests, 648 of them on every push, without a language model and without network.
bench.tests.takeaway: They include the recount of every published figure and the check that every legal basis in the rule set points to real official text.
bench.corpus.heading: Legal text per language
bench.corpus.text: individually citable passages, in German and in English with the same ids.
bench.limits.heading: What the figures do not show
bench.limits.1: No lawyer has reviewed the walkthrough.
bench.limits.2: The derived obligations are checked against the text of the regulation, but not measured against an outside standard; no official collection of examples exists for them.
bench.limits.3: The example descriptions are short. Anyone classifying their own system knows more than two sentences; the figure therefore tends to be too low rather than too high.
